title: Full, Free, and Fast
objectives: I can use the suffixes -ful, -less, and -ly to understand new words.
I can name the opposite when a word ends in -ful or -less.
I can use words that end in -ly to tell how an action happens.
I can write sentences with words from this unit to describe people and actions.
rationale: This unit follows the prefix unit so students see that word parts work at both ends of a word. The three suffixes carry one clear meaning each: -ful means full of, -less means without, and -ly tells in what way something happens. Pairs such as thoughtful and thoughtless and hopeful and hopeless reinforce the antonym thinking from unit 8, while gradually and swiftly introduce adverbs and give students a way to show how an action happens. Every word splits into a base the student already knows plus one suffix, so the routine is cover the ending, say the base, then say what the ending adds.

words.def: Caring about other people's feelings and showing it.
words.ex: It was thoughtful of Ben to save his friend a seat.
words.ex2: She wrote a thoughtful note to the new student.
words.nonExample: Grabbing the last cookie without asking is not thoughtful.

apps.academic: A thoughtful character shows care by noticing what others need.
apps.spoken: Thank you for the thoughtful gift.
apps.writing: Use thoughtful for kind actions that show you paid attention to someone.

cloze.s: The ___ boy noticed his friend was cold and lent him his warm jacket.

cloze2.s: Bringing soup to a sick neighbor was a ___ way to show she cared.

misuse.s: The thoughtful girl laughed at her friend's tears and walked away without caring.
misuse.why: Thoughtful means caring about feelings; laughing at tears is the opposite.

visual.alt: A child handing a note to a smiling friend.

words.def: Moving or acting in a smooth, beautiful way.
words.ex: The graceful dancer glided across the stage.
words.ex2: A swan floated in a graceful curve across the pond.
words.nonExample: A stumbling walk that bumps into chairs is not graceful.

apps.academic: A graceful movement in dance or sports flows without sudden jerks.
apps.spoken: The skater made a graceful turn on the ice.
apps.writing: Use graceful for smooth, beautiful movements.

cloze.s: The ___ swan glided across the pond without a single ripple.

cloze2.s: With a ___ leap, the dancer crossed the stage as if she were flying.

misuse.s: The graceful skater tripped over her own feet and crashed into the wall.
misuse.why: Graceful means smooth and beautiful; tripping and crashing is the opposite.

visual.alt: A swan gliding on water beside a dancer in a leap.

words.def: Calm and quiet, without fighting or noise.
words.ex: We sat on the peaceful beach and watched the waves.
words.ex2: After the storm, the town was peaceful again.
words.nonExample: A noisy argument in a crowded hallway is not peaceful.

apps.academic: A peaceful setting in a story often comes before a problem or after one is solved.
apps.spoken: It is so peaceful in the library.
apps.writing: Use peaceful for a calm place, a quiet mood, or a time without fighting.

cloze.s: After the long day, the baby fell asleep in the ___ quiet of the little room.

cloze2.s: The two countries agreed to a ___ solution instead of going to war.

misuse.s: The peaceful playground was full of shouting, fighting, and crashing noises.
misuse.why: Peaceful means calm and quiet; shouting and fighting are the opposite.

visual.alt: A quiet lake with a white dove flying overhead.

words.def: Not afraid of anything; very brave.
words.ex: The fearless firefighter ran into the smoky building to help.
words.ex2: A fearless little girl climbed to the top of the rock wall.
words.nonExample: A child who hides under the bed during thunder is not fearless.

apps.academic: A fearless character faces danger without stopping to worry.
apps.spoken: My sister is fearless on the high slide.
apps.writing: Use fearless for someone who faces danger without worry.

cloze.s: The ___ explorer stepped into the dark cave with only a small flashlight.

cloze2.s: With a ___ grin, the toddler walked right up to the huge dog and patted its head.

misuse.s: The fearless boy ran away from a tiny spider, screaming and shaking with worry.
misuse.why: Fearless means not afraid; running away screaming shows fear.

visual.alt: A child in a cape standing next to a lion.

words.def: Unable to stay still or calm; always moving.
words.ex: The restless puppy paced around the room all night.
words.ex2: Waiting for the movie to begin, the kids grew restless.
words.nonExample: A cat sleeping peacefully in the sun is not restless.

segs.m: a time of calm and stillness

apps.academic: A restless character cannot sit still and often wants to leave or begin something.
apps.spoken: I felt restless during the long ride.
apps.writing: Use restless to show that a character cannot settle down.

cloze.s: During the long car ride, the ___ children kicked their seats and asked how much farther it was.

cloze2.s: On the night before the trip, Lila felt too ___ to sleep and wandered around her room.

misuse.s: The restless boy sat perfectly still for three hours without moving a muscle.
misuse.why: Restless means unable to stay still; sitting perfectly still is the opposite.

visual.alt: A puppy pacing near a clock on the wall.

words.def: So valuable that no amount of money could buy it.
words.ex: The museum guards the priceless painting night and day.
words.ex2: To Grandma, her old photographs are priceless.
words.nonExample: A pencil that costs one dime is not priceless.

segs.m: the amount of money something costs

apps.academic: A priceless object, such as an ancient treasure, cannot be replaced.
apps.spoken: That family photo is priceless to me.
apps.writing: Use priceless for something so valuable that no price is enough.

cloze.s: The ancient crown in the museum was ___ because there was nothing else like it in the world.

cloze2.s: For the little girl, her grandfather's old watch was a ___ treasure that no money could replace.

misuse.s: The priceless toy was free from the trash can and nobody wanted it at all.
misuse.why: Priceless means too valuable to buy; trash that nobody wants is not priceless.

visual.alt: A shining jewel next to a framed painting.

words.def: Perfect, with no mistakes or damage.
words.ex: The gymnast gave a flawless performance on the beam.
words.ex2: Her flawless handwriting looked like it came from a printer.
words.nonExample: A drawing with smudges and torn corners is not flawless.

apps.academic: A flawless diamond has no scratches or cloudy spots.
apps.spoken: The pianist played a flawless song.
apps.writing: Use flawless for work or objects with no mistakes at all.

cloze.s: The jeweler held up a ___ diamond without a single scratch or cloudy spot.

cloze2.s: Her speech was ___: she did not stumble, forget a line, or lose her place.

misuse.s: His flawless drawing had smudges, torn corners, and crooked lines all over the page.
misuse.why: Flawless means perfect; smudges and crooked lines are flaws.

visual.alt: A sparkling gem with a gold star next to it.

words.def: Having no chance of getting better or working out.
words.ex: The lost hiker felt hopeless until he heard a whistle in the distance.
words.ex2: It seemed hopeless to fix the broken kite, but Dad found some tape.
words.nonExample: Feeling sure that a plan will work is not hopeless.

segs.m: a wish that things will turn out well

apps.academic: A hopeless situation in a story often turns around when a character finds help.
apps.spoken: It felt hopeless until my friend offered to help.
apps.writing: Use hopeless for a feeling or a situation with no sign of improvement.

cloze.s: After searching for hours in the thick fog, the climbers felt ___ about finding the trail.

cloze2.s: The team was losing by thirty points, and the game looked ___ with only one minute left.

misuse.s: He felt hopeless because he was sure that everything would turn out great.
misuse.why: Hopeless means no chance of success; being sure everything will be great is the opposite.

visual.alt: A sad hiker standing alone in thick fog.

words.frame: Things can feel hopeless when ___, but ___.

words.def: Little by little, slowly over time.
words.ex: The sky gradually turned from black to pink as the sun rose.
words.ex2: Gradually, the shy new student made friends.
words.nonExample: A sudden crash is not something that happens gradually.

segs.m: happening slowly, a little at a time

apps.academic: In science, a seed gradually grows into a plant over many days.
apps.spoken: Gradually, I got better at the piano.
apps.writing: Use gradually to show change that happens over time.

cloze.s: As the sun rose, the dark sky ___ turned pink and then gold.

cloze2.s: The little boy ___ learned to swim, starting with kicks and ending with strokes.

misuse.s: The ice cream gradually melted in one second and was gone in a flash.
misuse.why: Gradually means little by little; melting in one second is sudden.

visual.alt: A sunrise that slowly brightens beside a growing seedling.

words.ex: The cheetah swiftly chased the antelope across the field.
words.ex2: She swiftly packed her bag when she heard the bell.
words.nonExample: Crawling at a snail's pace is not moving swiftly.

apps.academic: A river can flow swiftly after heavy rain.
apps.writing: Use swiftly to show that an action happens with speed.

cloze.s: As the storm came near, the sailor ___ lowered the sails and tied them down.

cloze2.s: The hawk dove ___ from the sky and caught the mouse in a heartbeat.

misuse.s: The turtle swiftly crawled across the road at the slowest speed it could manage.
misuse.why: Swiftly means very quickly; the slowest speed is the opposite.

visual.alt: A hawk diving fast with wind lines behind it.

passage.title: The Night of the Lanterns
paras: On the night of the lantern festival, the village by the river was peaceful. Mei carried a paper lantern that her grandmother had made. To Mei, it was priceless. Each fold was flawless and perfectly sharp, and a tiny candle glowed inside like a small star.

At the riverbank, Mei grew restless, waiting for the signal. A thoughtful neighbor handed her a warm cup of tea. Gradually, the sky grew dark, and the first lanterns floated onto the water in a graceful line.

Mei's little brother, Kai, was fearless. He stepped to the edge of the dock to set his lantern on the river. Then a gust tipped it, and it began to sink. For a moment the situation seemed hopeless. Swiftly, Mei knelt and scooped the lantern up with both hands.
Kai hugged her and whispered thank you. Together they set the lantern back on the water, and its glow drifted slowly away down the river while the villagers clapped.

qs.why: The lantern was made by Mei's grandmother, so it meant more to her than money could measure.

qs.q: Why did Mei grow restless at the riverbank?
choices: She was afraid of the river.
She was waiting for the signal and could not stay still.
qs.why: The text says she was waiting for the signal, and restless means unable to stay calm.

qs.q: Which detail shows that Kai was fearless?
choices: He stepped to the edge of the dock to set his lantern on the river.
He drank a cup of tea.
qs.why: Stepping to the edge of the dock shows he was not afraid of the water.

qs.q: Which sentence tells the main idea?
choices: Lanterns are never safe on water.
Tea is served at every festival.
Mei acted quickly to save her brother's lantern during a festival.
qs.why: The passage builds toward Mei scooping up the lantern and saving it.

teacher.overview: Students use the suffixes -ful (full of), -less (without), and -ly (in a way) to understand ten words. They split each word into base and suffix, read a narrative in which the words appear, pair opposites, and write sentences that use the words.

notes.va.thoughtful.adj: Thoughtful = thought + -ful, full of caring thoughts for others. Do not confuse with thinking hard about a math problem; here it means kind and attentive.
notes.va.graceful.adj: Graceful = grace + -ful. Link to clumsy from unit 1 as the opposite. Ask students to move gracefully across the room, then clumsily, and describe the difference.
notes.va.peaceful.adj: Peaceful = peace + -ful. It can describe a place or a way of solving a problem. Contrast with gloomy and restless from other units.
notes.va.fearless.adj: Fearless = fear + -less, without fear. Contrast with timid from unit 1. Note that a fearless person is not always wise; ask when brave and careful should go together.
notes.va.restless.adj: Restless = rest + -less, without rest. Compare it with uneasy from unit 5: uneasy is worry, restless is the need to move.
notes.va.priceless.adj: Priceless = price + -less, so students may guess it means worthless. Clear that up: it means without a price because no price is enough. This is the trickiest -less word.
notes.va.flawless.adj: Flawless = flaw + -less. Ask students whether a flawless performance is the goal in school or whether learning from mistakes matters more.
notes.va.hopeless.adj: Hopeless = hope + -less. Pair with hopeful as the opposite. Be sensitive: talk about turning a hopeless feeling around by asking for help.
notes.va.gradually.adv: Gradually = gradual + -ly. Adverbs tell how, when, or how much. Show a drawing where a plant grows in four small steps and use gradually to describe it.
notes.va.swiftly.adv: Swiftly = swift + -ly. Link back to sprint from unit 7: a runner sprints, a bird flies swiftly. Ask for gradually and swiftly as an opposite pair in action.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'I see the word fearless. I cover -less and I see fear. Fear means being afraid, and -less means without. So fearless means without fear, or not afraid. I check it against the sentence about the firefighter. It makes sense.'
discuss: Which -ful word describes a person you admire? Which -less word describes a place or a thing?
Why do you think some -less words, like priceless, mean something good?
misconceptions: Priceless means worthless because it ends in -less.
Words that end in -ly always tell how fast something moves.
extend: Make a word wall of -ful and -less pairs (hopeful and hopeless, careful and careless) with a sentence for each.
Rewrite a short paragraph by adding -ly words that show how each action happens.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Two days later, give students three new base words (such as help, fear, quick) and ask them to add -ful, -less, or -ly where it makes a real word. Revisit uneasy, reunite, and gloomy by asking students to describe a scene using an unit 5 word and one of these.

frames: The word ___ means ___ because the suffix -___ means ___.
wida.oral: Partner A says a base word such as hope, fear, or swift. Partner B adds a suffix, says the new word, and tells what it means.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (considerado, elegante, tranquilo, intrépido, agitado, invaluable, impecable, desesperado, rápidamente) are not reviewed by a native speaker; elegante for graceful is a loose match.
Priceless is the one -less word that means something very good; the teacher note flags it as a likely confusion.
Check that restless and uneasy remain distinct for third graders (need to move versus worry).
